anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: Which three bones fuse to form each hip bone, and where do they meet?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: The ilium, ischium & pubis, fused at the acetabulum (via the triradiate cartilage until puberty).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: How do the bones of the pelvic ring articulate?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: The hip bones join the sacrum at the sacroiliac joints posteriorly and each other at the pubic symphysis anteriorly.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: Distinguish the greater (false) from the lesser (true) pelvis.
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: The greater pelvis lies above the pelvic inlet (part of the abdominal cavity); the lesser pelvis lies below it and contains the pelvic viscera and birth canal.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: What are the borders of the pelvic inlet (brim)?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: Posterior = sacral promontory & ala; lateral = linea terminalis (arcuate line + pectineal line); anterior = pubic symphysis & crest.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: What is the linea terminalis composed of?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: The arcuate line of the ilium plus the pectineal line (pecten pubis) of the superior pubic ramus — the lateral border of the pelvic inlet.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: What are the borders of the pelvic outlet?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: Posterior = tip of the coccyx; lateral = ischial tuberosities; posterolateral = sacrotuberous ligaments; anterior = pubic arch.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: What is the obstetric conjugate, and why can't it be measured directly?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: The distance from the sacral promontory to the most posterosuperior point of the pubic symphysis — the narrowest fixed AP inlet diameter (~10.5 cm); it lies behind the symphysis so is estimated from the diagonal conjugate (~1.5–2 cm longer, measured per vaginam). The true (anatomical) conjugate runs to the superior symphyseal margin and is slightly longer.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: Which is usually the narrowest part of the whole birth canal?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: The interspinous distance — between the two ischial spines.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: Give three features distinguishing the female from the male pelvis.
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: The female pelvis has a wider subpubic angle (>80°, U-shaped), a rounder/oval inlet, a wider greater sciatic notch (~90°), everted ischial spines and a shallower cavity.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: Name the four Caldwell–Moloy pelvic shapes.
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: Gynaecoid (round, ideal for delivery), android (heart-shaped/male), anthropoid (oval, long AP) and platypelloid (flat, wide transverse).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: Where does the sacrospinous ligament attach?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: From the sacrum & coccyx to the ischial spine.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: Where does the sacrotuberous ligament attach?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: From the sacrum & coccyx to the ischial tuberosity.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: What do the sacrospinous and sacrotuberous ligaments create?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: They convert the greater & lesser sciatic notches into the greater & lesser sciatic foramina (and resist backward rotation of the sacrum).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: What is the functional difference between the greater and lesser sciatic foramina?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: The greater is the main exit from the pelvis to the gluteal region; the lesser is the route into the perineum (the pudendal nerve & internal pudendal vessels hook around the ischial spine to re-enter here).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: What is the key landmark within the greater sciatic foramen?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: Piriformis — structures pass above or below it.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: What exits ABOVE piriformis in the greater sciatic foramen?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: The superior gluteal nerve & vessels.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: List the structures exiting BELOW piriformis.
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: Inferior gluteal nerve & vessels, the sciatic nerve, posterior femoral cutaneous nerve, nerve to quadratus femoris, pudendal nerve & internal pudendal vessels, and the nerve to obturator internus.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: What passes through the lesser sciatic foramen?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: The tendon of obturator internus, the nerve to obturator internus, and the pudendal nerve & internal pudendal vessels re-entering the perineum.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: Which muscle forms the lateral wall of the pelvis, and what canal lies there?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: Obturator internus (with obturator fascia & membrane); the obturator canal transmits the obturator nerve & vessels to the thigh.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: Which muscle forms the posterior pelvic wall, and what lies on it?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: Piriformis — the sacral plexus lies on its anterior surface.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: What muscles make up the pelvic floor (pelvic diaphragm)?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: Levator ani (puborectalis, pubococcygeus & iliococcygeus) plus coccygeus (ischiococcygeus).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: From where does levator ani arise?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: From the tendinous arch (a thickening of obturator fascia) running from the pubis to the ischial spine.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: What is the nerve supply of levator ani?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: The nerve to levator ani (S3–S4) and branches of the pudendal nerve.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: What are the two hiatuses in the pelvic floor?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: The urogenital hiatus (urethra ± vagina) and the anal hiatus (anal canal).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: How does puborectalis contribute to continence?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: It forms a sling around the anorectal junction maintaining the anorectal angle (~80–90°); relaxation opens the angle to allow defecation.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: What is the perineal body?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: The central tendon of the perineum — a fibromuscular node anterior to the anal canal where the pelvic floor and perineal muscles converge; the key structure torn in a perineal tear / cut in an episiotomy.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: Classify the sacroiliac joint.
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: A compound joint: part synovial (anteriorly) and part syndesmosis (the strong posterior interosseous ligament); very stable with little movement.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: Classify the pubic symphysis and describe its behaviour in pregnancy.
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: A secondary cartilaginous joint (fibrocartilage disc); relaxin loosens it (and the SI joints) in pregnancy to widen the outlet (can cause symphysis pubis dysfunction).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: Why is the pelvic floor clinically important in women?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: Damage (childbirth, pudendal injury) causes pelvic organ prolapse and stress urinary incontinence.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.front: The ovarian/testicular (gonadal) arteries arise from the aorta at which level?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.back: At ~L2, just inferior to the renal arteries — they then descend on the posterior abdominal wall to the gonads.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: What is the trigone of the bladder?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: A smooth triangular area of the bladder base bounded by the two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice; it is sensitive to stretch.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: What is the median umbilical ligament?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: The fibrous remnant of the urachus, running from the apex of the bladder to the umbilicus.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: What muscle forms the bladder wall, and what is the retropubic space?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: The detrusor (smooth muscle); the retropubic space (of Retzius) is the extraperitoneal fat-filled space between the bladder and the pubic symphysis.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: Describe the two urethral sphincters.
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: The internal urethral sphincter (smooth muscle at the bladder neck; involuntary, prevents retrograde ejaculation in the male) and the external urethral sphincter (skeletal muscle in the deep perineal pouch; voluntary, pudendal nerve).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: What is the effect of PARASYMPATHETIC stimulation on the bladder?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: Detrusor contracts and the internal sphincter relaxes → voiding (“S2,3,4 empties the bladder”).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: What is the effect of SYMPATHETIC stimulation on the bladder?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: Detrusor relaxes and the internal sphincter contracts → storage/continence (and prevents retrograde ejaculation).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: Where does the ureter cross into the pelvis?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: At the bifurcation of the common iliac artery, over the pelvic brim; it then runs down the lateral pelvic wall.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: Name the three sites of ureteric constriction.
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: The pelviureteric junction (PUJ), where it crosses the pelvic brim/iliac vessels, and the vesicoureteric junction (VUJ) — the narrowest.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: Describe the relationship of the ureter to the uterine artery, and its significance.
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: The uterine artery crosses anterior (superior) to the ureter near the cervix (“water under the bridge”) — the ureter is at risk of ligation during hysterectomy.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: Why does the ureter pierce the bladder wall obliquely?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: The oblique passage acts as a physiological (flap) valve that is compressed as the bladder fills, preventing vesicoureteric reflux.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: Name the four parts of the male urethra in order.
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: Pre-prostatic → prostatic → membranous → spongy (penile).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: Which part of the male urethra is the widest, and which the least distensible?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: The prostatic part is widest (receives the ejaculatory ducts); the membranous part is shortest and least distensible (through the external sphincter) — the commonest site of iatrogenic injury.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: Why is the female more prone to ascending UTIs?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: The female urethra is short (~4 cm) and straight, allowing easier ascent of bacteria to the bladder.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: At what level does the rectum begin, and what is its dilated distal part called?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: At S3 (continuous with the sigmoid colon); the dilated distal portion is the ampulla.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: Describe the peritoneal covering of the rectum.
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: Peritoneum covers the upper third anteriorly & laterally, the middle third anteriorly only, and the lower third is subperitoneal (no peritoneum).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: Give the arterial supply of the rectum.
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: Superior rectal (from the inferior mesenteric artery), middle rectal (from the internal iliac) and inferior rectal (from the internal pudendal) arteries.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: What is the clinical significance of the pectinate (dentate) line?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: It divides the anal canal: above = visceral (autonomic) innervation, insensate, portal venous drainage, columnar epithelium (internal, painless haemorrhoids); below = somatic (inferior rectal) innervation, very sensitive, systemic drainage, squamous epithelium (external, painful haemorrhoids/fissures).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: Name the three parts of the uterus.
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: The fundus, body (containing the cavity) and cervix.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: Name the three layers of the uterine wall.
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: Endometrium (mucosa, shed in menstruation), myometrium (smooth muscle) and perimetrium (peritoneal serosa).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: What is the normal position of the uterus?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: Anteverted (the cervix tips forward relative to the vagina) and anteflexed (the body is flexed forward on the cervix).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: Name the parts of the uterine (Fallopian) tube from lateral to medial.
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: Infundibulum (with fimbriae) → ampulla → isthmus → intramural (uterine) part.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: Where does fertilisation usually occur, and where is the commonest site of ectopic pregnancy?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: Both in the ampulla of the uterine tube.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: What does the suspensory ligament of the ovary carry?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: The ovarian vessels (and nerves/lymphatics) — it runs from the ovary to the pelvic side wall over the brim; the ovarian ligament tethers the ovary to the uterus.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: Describe the blood supply of the uterus and vagina.
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: The uterine artery (from the internal iliac) supplies the uterus and, via the vaginal artery, the vagina; it anastomoses with the ovarian artery (from the aorta).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: What is the round ligament of the uterus, and its course?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: A remnant of the gubernaculum running from the uterine horn, through the deep inguinal ring & inguinal canal, to the labium majus (helps maintain anteversion).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: What is the broad ligament?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: A double fold of peritoneum draping over the uterus, tubes & ovaries — subdivided into the mesometrium, mesosalpinx & mesovarium.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: What are the true structural supports of the cervix/uterus?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: The transverse cervical (cardinal) and uterosacral ligaments (condensations of endopelvic fascia).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: What is the rectouterine pouch, and why is it important?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: The pouch of Douglas (between uterus & rectum) — the lowest point of the peritoneal cavity in the female; fluid/blood/pus collects here and can be sampled via the posterior vaginal fornix (culdocentesis).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: Which zone of the prostate gives rise to most cancers, and which to BPH?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: The peripheral zone (posterior) → most carcinomas (palpable on PR); the transitional (periurethral) zone → benign prostatic hyperplasia.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.front: How is the ejaculatory duct formed, and where does it open?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.back: By the union of the ductus (vas) deferens and the duct of the seminal vesicle; it opens into the prostatic urethra (at the seminal colliculus).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.question: Each hip bone is formed by the fusion of which three bones?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.explanation: The ilium, ischium and pubis fuse at the acetabulum to form each hip bone (os coxae).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.question: Which structure forms the lateral border of the pelvic inlet (brim)?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.explanation: The lateral border of the pelvic inlet is the linea terminalis — the arcuate line of the ilium plus the pectineal line of the pubis.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.question: Which of the following forms the POSTERIOR border of the pelvic outlet?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.explanation: The pelvic outlet is bounded posteriorly by the tip of the coccyx (the sacral promontory is the posterior border of the inlet).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.question: The narrowest part of the birth canal is usually the distance between:
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.explanation: The interspinous (ischial spine to ischial spine) distance is normally the narrowest part of the pelvic canal.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.question: The diagonal conjugate is measured clinically because:
options: The true (obstetric) conjugate cannot be measured directly
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.explanation: The true/obstetric conjugate lies behind the symphysis and cannot be measured per vaginam, so the diagonal conjugate (promontory to inferior symphysis) is measured and ~1.5–2 cm is subtracted.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.question: Which feature is characteristic of the FEMALE pelvis?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.explanation: The female pelvis has a wide, U-shaped subpubic angle (>80°), a rounder inlet, a wider sciatic notch and everted spines — adaptations for childbirth.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.question: The sacrospinous ligament runs from the sacrum/coccyx to the:
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.explanation: The sacrospinous ligament attaches to the ischial spine; the sacrotuberous ligament attaches to the ischial tuberosity.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.question: The sacrospinous and sacrotuberous ligaments together:
options: Convert the sciatic notches into the greater and lesser sciatic foramina
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.explanation: The two ligaments span the sciatic notches, converting them into the greater and lesser sciatic foramina.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.question: Which structure is the key landmark dividing the greater sciatic foramen?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.explanation: Piriformis passes through the greater sciatic foramen; structures are described as passing above or below it.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.question: Which nerve/vessel exits ABOVE piriformis in the greater sciatic foramen?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.explanation: Only the superior gluteal nerve and vessels pass above piriformis; everything else (sciatic, inferior gluteal, pudendal, etc.) passes below.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.question: The pudendal nerve re-enters the perineum by passing through which structure?
options: The lesser sciatic foramen (around the ischial spine)
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.explanation: The pudendal nerve leaves via the greater sciatic foramen, hooks around the ischial spine/sacrospinous ligament, and re-enters the perineum through the lesser sciatic foramen.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.question: The obturator canal transmits which structures to the thigh?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.explanation: The obturator canal (at the superolateral obturator foramen) transmits the obturator nerve and vessels to the medial thigh.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.question: The pelvic diaphragm is composed of which muscles?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.explanation: The pelvic floor (pelvic diaphragm) is formed by levator ani (puborectalis, pubococcygeus, iliococcygeus) and coccygeus.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.question: Which part of levator ani forms a sling that maintains the anorectal angle?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.explanation: Puborectalis slings around the anorectal junction, maintaining the ~80–90° anorectal angle essential for faecal continence.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.question: The pelvic floor muscles are innervated principally by which spinal levels?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.explanation: Levator ani and the perineal muscles are supplied by S2–S4 (nerve to levator ani and the pudendal nerve).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.question: The pubic symphysis is classified as which type of joint?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.explanation: The pubic symphysis is a secondary cartilaginous joint (symphysis) with a fibrocartilage disc between hyaline-lined pubic bodies.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.question: Which hormone loosens the pelvic joints during pregnancy?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.explanation: Relaxin loosens the pubic symphysis and sacroiliac joints in pregnancy to increase pelvic diameters for delivery.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.question: A muscle forming the lateral wall of the pelvis is:
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.explanation: Obturator internus, covered by obturator fascia, forms the lateral wall of the pelvis; piriformis forms the posterior wall.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.question: The perineal body is clinically important because it is:
options: The origin of the sciatic nerve
The central tendon torn in a perineal tear / cut in an episiotomy
A branch of the internal iliac artery
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.explanation: The perineal body is the fibromuscular central tendon where the pelvic floor and perineal muscles meet — the key structure damaged in obstetric perineal tears and episiotomy.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.question: The sacroiliac joint is best described as:
options: Part synovial and part syndesmosis, very stable
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.explanation: The SI joint is a compound joint — synovial anteriorly and a syndesmosis (interosseous ligament) posteriorly — designed for stability and weight transfer with minimal movement.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.question: Weakness or injury of the pelvic floor most characteristically causes:
options: Pelvic organ prolapse and stress incontinence
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.explanation: Pelvic floor damage (childbirth, pudendal injury) leads to pelvic organ prolapse and stress urinary incontinence.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.question: Which of the following passes through the LESSER sciatic foramen?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology &.explanation: The lesser sciatic foramen transmits the obturator internus tendon, the nerve to obturator internus, and the pudendal neurovascular bundle re-entering the perineum.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.question: The trigone of the bladder is bounded by which structures?
options: The two ureteric orifices and the apex
The two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice
The internal and external urethral orifices
The median and medial umbilical ligaments
The ureteric orifices and the ejaculatory ducts
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.explanation: The trigone is the smooth triangular area between the two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.question: Parasympathetic (S2–S4) stimulation of the bladder produces:
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.explanation: Parasympathetic pelvic splanchnic (S2–4) activity contracts the detrusor and relaxes the sphincter → voiding. Sympathetic activity stores urine.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.question: Sympathetic innervation of the bladder promotes continence by:
options: Relaxing the detrusor and contracting the internal sphincter
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.explanation: Sympathetic (L1–2, hypogastric) fibres relax the detrusor and contract the internal urethral sphincter — storage/continence.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.question: The ureter enters the pelvis by crossing over the:
options: Bifurcation of the common iliac artery
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.explanation: The ureter crosses the pelvic brim at the bifurcation of the common iliac artery, then descends on the lateral pelvic wall.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.question: Which is the NARROWEST point of the ureter, where stones most often impact?
options: Where it crosses the pelvic brim
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.explanation: The vesicoureteric junction (VUJ) is the narrowest of the three constrictions (PUJ, pelvic brim, VUJ).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.question: During a hysterectomy the ureter is at risk because:
options: It runs anterior to the uterine artery
The uterine artery crosses anterior/superior to it ('water under the bridge')
It lies within the broad ligament mesovarium
It passes through the inguinal canal
It is fused to the cervix
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.explanation: The uterine artery crosses superior (anterior) to the ureter near the cervix — 'water (ureter) under the bridge (artery)' — so the ureter can be clamped/ligated during hysterectomy.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.question: The oblique passage of the ureter through the bladder wall functions to:
options: Act as a valve preventing vesicoureteric reflux
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.explanation: The oblique intramural course is compressed as the bladder fills, forming a flap valve that prevents reflux of urine up the ureter.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.question: Which part of the male urethra is the shortest and least distensible?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.explanation: The membranous urethra passes through the external urethral sphincter; it is the shortest and least distensible, and a common site of injury.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.question: Fertilisation and the commonest site of ectopic pregnancy are both in the:
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.explanation: Fertilisation normally occurs in the ampulla of the uterine tube, which is also the commonest site of a tubal ectopic pregnancy.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.question: The three layers of the uterine wall from inside out are:
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.explanation: From inner to outer: endometrium (mucosa), myometrium (smooth muscle) and perimetrium (peritoneum).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.question: The normal uterus is described as:
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.explanation: The typical uterus is anteverted (cervix tips forward on the vagina) and anteflexed (body flexed forward on the cervix).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.question: The suspensory ligament of the ovary transmits the:
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.explanation: The suspensory ligament of the ovary (infundibulopelvic ligament) carries the ovarian artery, vein, nerves and lymphatics to the ovary.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.question: The uterine artery is a branch of the:
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.explanation: The uterine artery arises from the anterior division of the internal iliac artery; the ovarian artery (from the aorta) anastomoses with it.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.question: The lowest point of the peritoneal cavity in the female, where fluid collects, is the:
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.explanation: The rectouterine pouch (of Douglas), between the uterus and rectum, is the lowest point of the female peritoneal cavity and can be sampled via the posterior fornix.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.question: The round ligament of the uterus ends in the:
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.explanation: The round ligament (a gubernaculum remnant) runs from the uterine horn through the deep inguinal ring and inguinal canal to the labium majus.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.question: Most prostate carcinomas arise in which zone?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.explanation: Most prostate cancers arise in the peripheral (posterior) zone, which is why they are palpable on digital rectal examination; BPH affects the transitional zone.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.question: Benign prostatic hyperplasia characteristically involves which zone, causing what?
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.explanation: BPH affects the transitional/periurethral zone, compressing the prostatic urethra and causing bladder outflow obstruction (hesitancy, poor stream, nocturia).

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.question: The ejaculatory duct is formed by the union of the ductus deferens with the duct of the:
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.explanation: The ductus (vas) deferens joins the seminal vesicle duct to form the ejaculatory duct, which opens into the prostatic urethra.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.question: The pectinate line is clinically important because ABOVE it the anal canal is:
options: Autonomically innervated and insensate, draining to the portal system
Supplied by the inferior rectal artery
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.explanation: Above the pectinate line: visceral (autonomic) innervation (insensate), portal venous drainage and columnar epithelium — hence painless internal haemorrhoids.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.question: The superior rectal artery, supplying the upper rectum, is a branch of the:
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.explanation: The superior rectal artery is the continuation of the inferior mesenteric artery; the middle rectal arises from the internal iliac and the inferior rectal from the internal pudendal.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.question: A short, straight urethra explains why women are more prone to:
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.explanation: The female urethra is only ~4 cm and straight, allowing bacteria to ascend easily and predisposing to UTIs.

anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.question: The median umbilical ligament represents the remnant of the:
anatomy__PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Or.explanation: The median umbilical ligament is the fibrous remnant of the urachus, connecting the bladder apex to the umbilicus.
